turn_text: What's your sense or your confidence in some of these lawsuits actually being successful or actually bringing about change for the industry?

Yeah, the challenge with these lawsuits is they are lawsuits that take a decade to decide. Between the time that the lawsuit is filed, you've got one administration in office. And then you've got two or three by the time that the case is finally decided by the Supreme Court one way or the other. The Supreme Court may deny cert or it may accept cert. But that whole process can take eight to 10 years. And so a lot of the harm that has been done is really old news by the time that we get around to deciding the case. And a lot of times the companies see the futility of moving forward. And so they'll settle in some way beforehand. But I think that the challenge with that length of time is keeping the new administration, whatever that is, focused and not subject to the political pressures that would alter the focus on the case.

I do want to talk about AI. I know that in June, you and some of your colleagues introduced a bill that would create a National Commission on Artificial Intelligence. I'm curious to hear kind of how you envision that being different from some of these other commissions that have been set up in recent years, like the National AI Advisory Committee, the National Security Commission on AI. How would this body be different?

Obviously, the state legislatures are going to have some role, but primarily it's going to be Congress. And so to have a body that involves members of Congress, especially leadership in Congress, and to have the experts mingling with the legislators in that context, I think is really important to make sure that we pass the right laws so that the administration can pass the right regulations to govern this new area, a new area that has huge potential for good and also is really scary in a lot of ways to people.

turn_text: I'm going to ask a cynical question. I can't imagine I'm the first cynical journalist you've encountered. But I was talking with a former Commerce official, not about AI, on something else. And the point that they made is, you know, A committee or a task force is kind of what Washington does when it's not sure what else to do. Is that where we are on AI? Is there not enough clarity on what we should be doing that the best thing Washington can do at this point is to set up kind of a commission or committee?

Well, you know, it's great. I would give you that same quote if it were related to budget issues, for example. When it comes to hard decisions, Congress wants to kick the ball down the road, kick the can down the road. And so we set up a committee and then we say, in next Congress, we're going to take up the recommendations from this committee. So it's really not our fault, and when we run for re-election, we can say, you know, we're doing everything we can. We've got a committee studying this issue. Simpson Bowles is a perfect example of that. It was a committee. Everybody ran and said, you know, I'm going to wait for the results from Simpson Bowles. And then very little happened that came from that very good hardworking group. In this case, I think it's a little bit different. I think what we're talking about with AI is really an unknown. And we've got so many issues, whether it's the Trump indictments. whether it's the oversight of the Biden administration with Hunter Biden, whether it's the dealing with inflation, dealing with the border. There are so many issues that Congress is dealing with right now that something that is unknown isn't going to rise to the top. If tomorrow we were concerned about Chinese hackers using AI to devastate the banking system in America, Absolutely. Congress would convene and we would bring experts in and we'd legislate and we'd give the administration authority and resources to deal with that. That's not this case right now. No one can identify that existential threat from AI. So in this case, I think it's important that we get people together that have the time and focus to address the AI issues in a thoughtful way. So I see the committee kicking the can down the road committee just a little bit different than what we're trying to do with AI.

Is there a question in your mind that you really want answered on AI or, you know, I wonder if there's like a, yeah, like a kind of the big outstanding question that you just haven't, don't feel you've gotten a good answer on.

Yeah, the main issue for me is how do we protect the public? AI is going to be used in the businesses, the capitalists, the inventors, the risk takers in this country are going to invent things with AI that are going to be used in the healthcare industry that are really almost miracles. They're huge advances and we're going to do the same thing with so many different sectors of our economy. But my question is, and those probably are best, they happen in an environment with less regulation rather than more regulation. The area I'm most concerned with is that kid that's contemplating suicide, how do we help that kid rather than teach that kid the most efficient way to accomplish his goal? And how do we make sure that we don't have body shaming for teenage girls that causes depression and anorexia and other issues? So all of those issues that we got wrong, frankly, with the internet, how do we make sure that we get them right with AI and we, as government officials, do our very best. to advance a new technology that has huge potential in a way that protects our citizens and really the world from an evil actor using AI in a terrible way.
